newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Aid to ex-Yugoslavia must be faster, summit hears.
newsitem.headline: Aid to ex-Yugoslavia must be faster, summit hears.

text.p: Bosnia told Central European leaders on Friday that if they want to send refugees back to their homeland they must give more help for post-war reconstruction.
And Croatia complained that it felt pressure to join an "artifical" association with other former Yugoslav republics from which it split with so much bitterness in 1991.
The heads of government of the 16-member Central European Initiative were meeting in the south Austrian town of Graz to discuss closer regional cooperation and security issues.

Austrian Chancellor Franz Vranitzky, the two-day summit's host, told reporters implementation of the U.S.-brokered Dayton peace accord, which ended 43 months of ethnic warfare in former Yugoslavia, was critical to the region.
"The Bosnian Prime Minister told us that if the economic cooperation with Bosnia is not stepped up, then the repatriation of refugees will remain a dream," Vranitzky said.
"Really, the world can do much," Bosnian Prime Minister Hasan Muratovic told Reuters. "There was a promise to extensively support Bosnia-Hercegovina's economic rehabilitation and reconstruction.
"Everybody knows that there will be no lasting peace without economic rehabilitation."
Croatia warned that the establishment of stronger regional ties might push the ex-Yugoslav republics into a renewed alliance.

"In spite of the multiple evidence of the impossibility of a joint state in the area of the former Yugoslavia in the 20th century, some agents of European policies are making repeated attempts to create some artificial associations and assign Croatia a place in it beforehand," Croatian Prime Minister Zlatko Matesa said in a speech.
"Croatia turns down any attempt to make it a party of some artificial political associations," he added.
The CEI on Friday admitted Moldova as its 16th member country.

Yugoslavia -- now a rump state consisting only of Serbia and Montenegro -- is the next, and last, candidate for the loosely-knit forum but instead of applying as a new member it has asked to return as one of the CEI's four 1989 founders.
"There can be no return because they are a different country now," Austrian Foreign Ministry official Rudolf Bogner told Reuters. "The other (successor republics) had to apply as well."

The summit received a letter from Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin suggesting dialogue with the CEI, which Moscow saw as "an important component of the European architecture of the 21st Century".
"There must be no security architecture without consultation with Russia," commented Vranitzky.
